events.title: Bush carries Arizona
events.text: George W. Bush carried Arizona by six points; it had voted Republican for president in every election since 1952 but one, 1996.

events.title: Napolitano elected
events.text: Janet Napolitano, a Democrat, beat Matt Salmon by 11,819 votes, without carrying Maricopa County.

events.title: Biggs in the House
events.text: Andy Biggs, a lawyer from Gilbert, began eight years in the Arizona House of Representatives.

events.title: Bush again
events.text: Bush carried Arizona a second time, by ten and a half points.

events.title: Napolitano re-elected
events.text: Napolitano won a second term with 62.6 percent, carrying every county.

events.title: McCain's home state
events.text: Senator John McCain, the Republican presidential nominee, carried Arizona by eight and a half points.

events.title: Brewer takes office
events.text: Napolitano resigned to become Secretary of Homeland Security; Secretary of State Jan Brewer, a Republican, became governor.

events.title: SB 1070 signed
events.text: On 23 April Brewer signed SB 1070, an immigration-enforcement law; in 2012 the Supreme Court upheld one provision and struck down three.

events.title: Brewer elected
events.text: Brewer beat the attorney general, Terry Goddard, by almost twelve points.

events.title: Biggs leads Senate
events.text: Biggs became president of the Arizona Senate, a post he held until 2017.

events.title: Ducey elected
events.text: Doug Ducey, a Republican, beat Fred DuVal by almost twelve points.

events.title: Trump by 3.5
events.text: Donald Trump carried Arizona by three and a half points.

events.title: Biggs to Congress
events.text: Biggs began representing Arizona's 5th District, in the East Valley, in the U.S. House.

events.title: Sinema wins Senate
events.text: Kyrsten Sinema became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race in Arizona since 1988.

events.title: McCain dies
events.text: Senator John McCain, the 2008 Republican presidential nominee, died on 25 August, at 81.

events.title: Hobbs elected
events.text: Katie Hobbs, a state senator and social worker, was elected secretary of state, the first Democrat in the post since 1995.

events.title: Freedom Caucus chair
events.text: Biggs became chair of the House Freedom Caucus, serving until 2022.

events.title: Biden by 10,457
events.text: Joe Biden carried Arizona by 10,457 votes, the first Democratic win for president there since 1996.

events.title: Navajo Nation votes
events.text: Precincts on the Navajo and Hopi reservations cast nearly 60,000 ballots, up from about 42,500 in 2016.

events.title: Results certified
events.text: On 30 November Hobbs, Governor Ducey, the attorney general and the chief justice certified the results.

events.title: Electoral objection
events.text: On 6 January Biggs voted for the objection to Arizona's electoral votes; it failed, 121 to 303.

events.title: Senate review
events.text: A review of Maricopa's 2020 ballots ordered by the state Senate began; its count found Biden's margin 360 votes wider.

events.title: Hobbs beats Lake
events.text: Hobbs beat Kari Lake by 17,117 votes, two-thirds of a point.

events.title: Cochise delay
events.text: Two Cochise County supervisors delayed certifying the results until a judge ordered them to.

events.title: Independents pass GOP again
events.text: Voters registered with no party again outnumbered Republicans, as they first had in 2014.

events.title: 143 vetoes
events.text: Facing a Republican legislature, Hobbs vetoed 143 bills, a single-session record.

events.title: 31 days at 110°F
events.text: Phoenix recorded 31 straight days at or above 110 degrees; Maricopa County counted 645 heat deaths that year.

events.title: 1864 ban repealed
events.text: On 2 May Hobbs signed the repeal of an 1864 law banning most abortions.

events.title: Trump and Gallego
events.text: Trump carried Arizona by five and a half points; on the same ballot Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, won the Senate seat by 2.4.

events.title: Props 139 and 314
events.text: Voters approved abortion rights in the constitution with 61.6 percent and a state border-crossing law with 62.6 percent.

events.title: Desert Guardian
events.text: On 25 February Hobbs created a border task force against cartels and smuggling, Operation Desert Guardian.

events.title: TSMC expands
events.text: TSMC raised its planned U.S. investment to $165 billion, building on its chip plants in north Phoenix.

events.title: Two endorsements
events.text: On 21 April President Trump endorsed both Biggs and Karrin Taylor Robson for governor.

events.title: Ag-to-Urban law
events.text: Hobbs signed a law letting farmers in the Phoenix and Pinal areas sell groundwater rights to homebuilders.

events.title: 174 vetoes
events.text: Hobbs vetoed 174 bills, breaking her own record.

events.title: Robson withdraws
events.text: On 12 February Robson ended her campaign, leaving Biggs the only candidate endorsed by Trump.

events.title: Budget signed
events.text: On 13 June Hobbs signed an $18.3 billion budget passed with votes from both parties.

events.title: Biggs wins primary
events.text: On 21 July Biggs won the Republican primary with 74 percent; Hobbs was unopposed.

events.title: No charges filed
events.text: The attorney general declined to charge Hobbs over donations from a group-home provider; a county inquiry continued.

events.title: Colorado River decision
events.text: The Interior Department set new river rules after the seven states failed to agree.

events.title: Debate without Hobbs
events.text: On 6 October Biggs debated the No Labels nominee, Teri Hourihan; Hobbs declined to take part.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: On 3 November Arizonans choose between Hobbs, Biggs, Hourihan and Lombardo.

eras: Napolitano, McCain and a Republican state
Hobbs, vetoes and a divided government
chartNote: Each state is coloured by the margin of the most recent presidential popular vote (Democratic minus Republican share of all votes; certified state results). It is a simplification: Arizona chooses its governor in its own race, and Arizonans split their tickets (in 2024 Donald Trump carried the state while a Democrat won its Senate seat), so the presidential colour is a backdrop, not a forecast. Shares are of land area, not of people or votes: about six in ten of Arizona's votes are cast in Maricopa County. Boundaries are today's states (Natural Earth); the map is framed on Arizona, so outer states are cut at the edge.
